faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Elizabeth basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Elizabethport basements the signs concentrate on the wall facing the water or the alley, and the entry is most often an old lateral or utility gap sealed with material that has long since rotted out. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: How is the price for a Elizabeth wildlife job figured?
faqs.a: By what the inspection finds: one squirrel entry at a gable vent is a short visit, while a raccoon family plus chewed fascia and fouled insulation is several. An Elmora single with squirrels at a dormer and a Peterstown twin with a basement rat run are both Elizabeth inspections, and the separate lines for removal, sealing, and cleanup show the owner where the money actually goes. We walk the property with you, point out each opening, and price the removal, the sealing, and any cleanup as separate lines before work starts.

Elizabeth.wildlife_intro:
Elizabeth is Union County's port city: Elizabethport's older blocks by the Arthur Kill, Peterstown and Bayway's working neighborhoods, North Elizabeth, and Elmora's more suburban streets. Rats are the city's first wildlife problem, working the port and industrial edges, the older sewers, and the blocks behind the food corridors. Raccoons den in the porch roofs and chimneys of the older housing in every section, opossums commute from the Elizabeth River banks, and starlings and sparrows fill the vents and signs along Broad Street and the avenues.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Elizabeth's attached and semi-attached rows share voids that animals treat as hallways, so entries are mapped across the connected rooflines and the plan assigns each one to its building.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Plainfield attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. The grand attics on the Crescent and Watchung streets are Plainfield's colony addresses, high, quiet, and entered at ridges the owners cannot see from the ground. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Plainfield home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. In the East End the returns end when the basement entries are mortared shut and the rear-yard food is locked down; trapping without those two halves has a perfect record of failure on these blocks. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

Plainfield.wildlife_intro:
Plainfield, the Queen City, is an older Union County city of substance: grand Victorians and colonials along the Watchung Avenue and Crescent Avenue streets, twins and apartments in the East End, and the West End's older blocks, all threaded by the Green Brook. Squirrels and raccoons work the big older homes, bats hold several of the grand attics, rats hold the downtown and East End basements, and groundhogs and skunks work the brook-side lots. The housing's age and size mean colonies and dens here run large before anyone notices.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Plainfield's big attics hide colonies well, so the survey here is measured in photographs and droppings maps, and cleanup scope is agreed before removal day, not discovered during it.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Union Township ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Battle Hill and Connecticut Farms the morning running usually enters at a corner where the original aluminum soffit has loosened, and the same corner fails on the neighboring houses within a few seasons. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Union Township garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. River-side Union lots give groundhogs a banked den and a garden in the same yard, and the trapping set goes at the bank burrow, not at the garden gate. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Union Township.wildlife_intro:
Union Township is a big, settled Union County suburb: Five Points and Union Center's older commercial-residential mix, Vauxhall's historic streets, Battle Hill's postwar homes, and the Elizabeth River and Route 22 corridors cutting through. Squirrels and raccoons are the township's daily work in the capes and colonials, groundhogs dig the river-side and field-edge lots, skunks work the lawns, rats appear around the corridor blocks, and bats take the quieter attics. The stock is mostly mid-century and aging in sync, soffits first.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. Union's mid-century subdivisions share builders and details, so a soffit entry here triggers a check of the whole original run, priced as a run rather than a patch.

faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Westfield home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. A Brightwood Tudor with a raccoon family in a stone chimney and a Boulevard colonial with squirrels at one gable are both routine Westfield calls, and their written quotes could hardly look less alike. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: Moles are tearing up my Westfield yard — how are they handled?
faqs.a: By trapping the active runs, not by poison peanuts or vibrating stakes, which mostly rearrange the damage. Surface ridges are feeding tunnels; the deep runs along edges and foundations are the travel lanes where traps belong. Westfield's groomed, irrigated lawns are grub habitat by design, and the spring mole ridging here follows the sprinkler layout with embarrassing precision. Eastern moles work most New Jersey lawns, and the star-nosed mole turns up in wetter ground. Expect a few visits spaced out — mole work is verified by fresh ridging stopping, not by a single day's catch.

Westfield.wildlife_intro:
Westfield is Union County's showcase suburb: a busy downtown, and around it streets of substantial colonials, Tudors, and Victorians on landscaped lots, with Mindowaskin Park and the Brightwood section's big homes at the top of the range. The canopy is mature and the houses are complex, so squirrels and raccoons are constant at the rooflines. Bats hold the larger attics, groundhogs work the park-side and brook-side lots, skunks dig the groomed lawns, and moles ridge them in spring. Westfield's wildlife problems arrive in well-kept packaging.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Westfield's canopy bridges to a great many rooflines, so the limb measurement is a standard line in the inspection report here, with the sealing plan drawn around it.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Cranford chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. The river-side chimneys host Cranford's spring litters, and the mothers pick the houses whose back yards run down to the water, which is most of the downtown. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Cranford lawn at night and it smells like skunk — what is going on?
faqs.a: Neat, cone-shaped holes in turf mean a skunk is mining grubs and earthworms, and late winter adds mating-season scent to the picture. Park-side Cranford lawns sit over rich, damp soil full of grubs, and the skunk digging maps the wet end of the yard where the larvae are thickest. The lasting answer is removing the den site and the food: we clear any skunk sheltering under steps or sheds, screen those voids, and talk through grub-heavy turf, because a lawn full of larvae gets visited nightly no matter how many skunks are taken off it.

Cranford.wildlife_intro:
Cranford is a Rahway River town with a postcard center: Victorian and colonial homes around the downtown, Nomahegan Park's lake and woods at the west end, and the river bending through the middle of everything. The river lots get the animals first, raccoons commuting up from the banks into chimneys, skunks and opossums under the porches, groundhogs in the banked yards. Squirrels work the street canopy into the eaves all over town, and bats hold attics in the older homes near the park. Cranford's charm and its wildlife pressure have the same source: water and old trees.

Decks and porches fail at ground level. The gap beneath a low deck is dark, dry, and sheltered enough for skunks, opossums, and groundhogs to den in, and lattice alone stops none of them. Lasting work means trenching around the structure and burying galvanized hardware cloth in an L-shape, so an animal digging at the edge meets mesh angled outward underground. Lattice or skirting goes back over the top for looks. It is unglamorous digging, and it is the difference between a den that stays empty and one that fills again every spring. Cranford's river-side decks are built over damp, shaded ground that animals love, and buried screening along the deck line is the town's most reliable single fix.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Rahway attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night scratching narrows the list: bats at dusk, flying squirrels gliding in after dark, raccoons moving heavily, or rats running a wall route. Daytime noise would point to gray squirrels instead. Rahway's river-park streets produce the night-noise calls, and the droppings usually decide between a raccoon commuting from the park woods and rats running the wall from the basement. Guessing wrong wastes money — the exits, timing, and sealing differ for each — so the inspection identifies the animal from droppings, entry size, and rub marks before any equipment is set.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a Rahway attic actually a fire risk?
faqs.a: They can be. Squirrels gnaw constantly to wear their teeth, and wiring, PVC, and stored paper are all fair game; chewed conductors in a hot attic are a genuine hazard, not a sales line. Rahway's older attics combine heavy squirrel traffic with wiring of several vintages, and chewed runs are photographed and flagged for the owner's electrician as a routine part of the job. Once the squirrels are out and the entries are meshed, we flag any chewed wiring we saw so an electrician can judge it — that check is part of why a squirrel job should never end at just closing the hole.

Rahway.wildlife_intro:
Rahway is an older river city between the suburbs: a historic downtown on the Rahway River, older singles and twins on the grid streets, postwar neighborhoods at the edges, and industry and Route 1 corridors adding hard edges. Rats work the older basements and the blocks behind the downtown and corridor food businesses. Raccoons den in the chimneys and porch roofs across the older sections, squirrels take the eaves along the river park, and groundhogs dig the park-side and field-edge lots. Rahway River Park gives the city a green spine and the animals a highway.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Rahway's corridor blocks get the food audit with the sealing, dumpsters, grease, and rear-yard storage named in the plan, because the river park supplies the animals and the corridors supply the meals.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Linden deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. Kill-side Linden gives opossums marsh cover and a row of low crawlspaces, and the vent screens on the water-facing side of the house are where the work concentrates. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

faqs.q: Do you charge to inspect a Linden attic?
faqs.a: The inspection is the working visit: roofline, attic, and foundation get checked, entries get photographed, and you receive a written quote for the full job. Linden inspections include the crawlspace circuit as standard, because in the older sections the under-house entries outnumber the roofline ones by a wide margin. That sequence — inspect first, quote in writing, then remove and seal — is how every job here runs, so there are no surprise line items after the animals are already out.

Linden.wildlife_intro:
Linden pairs heavy industry with settled neighborhoods: the Bayway refineries and the Arthur Kill on the east, and west of the tracks, older residential sections like Sunnyside with singles, twins, and small apartment buildings. Rats are the east side's constant and appear in the residential blocks behind the industry. Raccoons den throughout the older housing, opossums commute from the marshy Kill shore into the crawlspaces, and starlings and sparrows nest in the vents and signs along Wood and St. Georges avenues. The residential work is steady, unglamorous, and mostly at ground level.

Crawlspaces collect problems quietly. A vent screen rusts through, a pipe penetration was never sealed, and within a season the space underneath the house holds opossums, skunks, or a raccoon latrine — along with the odor that rides the ductwork upstairs. The fix starts with a light and a full circuit underneath: every vent screened in metal, gaps around plumbing and wiring sealed, and any carcass or waste taken out. Where moisture is part of the draw, we say so plainly, because a damp crawlspace keeps attracting animals no matter how well it is screened. Linden's crawlspaces near the Kill sit in damp ground, and the screening specification here assumes it, with the sill plate checked for softness on every circuit.
